I'm reading through this case report about a man with chronic meningococcemia and C7 complement deficiency, identifying the key entities to annotate like the disease, symptoms, and the family study showing heterozygous deficiency across generations.

"Chronic meningococcemia" is clearly a Specific Disease, appearing in both the title and the body. For "vasculitis" and "cutaneous vasculitis," I'm weighing whether these count as presenting features listed alongside fever and arthritis, which might mean they get routed to audit rather than annotated directly since they're generic category terms describing symptoms rather than the core diagnosis.

But the later mention "other causes of cutaneous vasculitis" feels different — it's referring to a whole family of conditions as an umbrella term, which pushes me toward annotating it as a Disease Class rather than skipping it.

Now I'm looking at "absence of the seventh component of complement" — C7 is a gene product, not a disease itself, but the title phrase might be naming the patient's condition (a complement deficiency state). I need to weigh whether "absence of" plus the protein name functions as a state-head construction denoting a deficiency disorder worth annotating.

Looking at sentence 3, "complete deficiency of the seventh component of complement" follows the same pattern and names the diagnosed condition, so this span also qualifies as a Specific Disease annotation.

I'm also considering "heterozygous deficiency of C7 in five members" — the prepositional object C7 is a gene product name, so "deficiency of C7" would be the annotated span, with "heterozygous" treated as a premodifier outside the span.

Then for "C7 deficiency" itself, I'm recognizing this fits the fixed N–N disease name exception — since the state term is a prenominal modifier of an enzyme/protein-bearing compound, it should keep its existing tagging as a Specific Disease rather than get re-annotated under the general rule.

Now I'm checking "absence of functional and antigenic C7" similarly — the state head "absence" takes the complement "of functional and antigenic C7," with C7 as the object being modified by "functional and antigenic."

I think the lab-finding phrase itself describes an assay result, while the real diagnostic claim is the "compatible with a complete deficiency" statement that follows. I'll lean toward annotating the title and the deficiency statement as the disease mention, while treating "absence of functional and antigenic C7" as more of an assay-based finding that likely falls under the exclusion rather than a separate disease annotation.

For the "heterozygous deficiency of C7 in five members" phrase, I'm weighing whether to include "heterozygous" as part of the span or start at "deficiency." Since the rule anchors the span at the state head noun and extends through the prepositional object, I'll annotate "deficiency of C7" as the Specific Disease mention, treating "heterozygous" as a modifier describing the carrier status rather than part of the core disease span.

Now turning to sentence 4's "Chronic neisserial infection" — I'm trying to determine if "infection" here functions as a generic category head modified by the taxon "neisserial," and whether the associative phrasing "can be associated with C7 deficiency" signals this is a broader disease class term rather than a specific diagnosis, since neisserial infections could span multiple distinct conditions like meningococcal disease.

I'm leaning toward annotating it as a Disease Class since it's describing a general category of Neisseria-related infections rather than a singular diagnosed condition, with the "chronic" qualifier not overriding this classification, similar to how "chronic meningococcemia" is treated as a classical example elsewhere.

For "cutaneous vasculitis" in the phrase about distinguishing from other causes, I'm marking this as Disease Class too since it represents a superordinate category of disorders rather than a specific diagnosis, while "C7 deficiency" nearby gets tagged as a Specific Disease span. I'm now looking at the title sentence describing absence of the seventh complement component in a patient presenting with chronic meningococcemia.

For the title phrase "Absence of the seventh component of complement," I'm treating "absence" as a valid state head similar to "deficiency," with the span extending through "the seventh component of complement" since that names a specific gene product. I'm now weighing how to handle "functional and antigenic C7" — whether these assay-type modifiers on the named gene product C7 push it toward being excluded as a measured quantity rather than annotated as a disease-related entity.

I'll annotate the clear diagnostic terms — the title, "complete deficiency of the seventh component of complement," "heterozygous deficiency of C7," and "C7 deficiency." For "absence of functional and antigenic C7," since this describes assay results rather than naming the condition itself, I'll treat it as falling under the measurement exclusion and skip annotating it, accepting the risk of missing a potential gold entity.

Moving to the next sentence, I'm identifying "chronic meningococcemia" as a Specific Disease while treating accompanying symptoms like fever, arthritis, and cutaneous vasculitis as presenting features to exclude. I'll also skip "presenting as vasculitis" in the title under the same audit logic.

For "heterozygous deficiency of C7 in five members," I'm settling on the span "heterozygous deficiency of C7" as the disease annotation, leaving out "in five members," though I'm weighing whether this carrier state should instead fall under the audit exclusion since it describes family members rather than a diagnosed patient.

Now I'm cataloging additional spans: "Chronic neisserial infection" and "cutaneous vasculitis" as Disease Class entries, "C7 deficiency" as Specific Disease, and "deficiency of the seventh component of complement" as another Specific Disease span.
